name: Quantum physics and the photoelectric effect

questions.q: What is a photon defined as in quantum physics?
a: A discrete packet (quantum) of electromagnetic radiation energy
A subatomic particle with positive charge and zero rest mass
A continuous wave of sound energy

questions.q: What equation gives the energy E of a photon in terms of Planck constant h and frequency f?
What is the threshold frequency f_0 in the photoelectric effect?
a: The maximum frequency of emitted photoelectrons
The frequency of incident light required to heat up the metal surface
The minimum frequency of incident radiation below which no photoelectrons are emitted from the metal surface
The frequency of the incident photon after collision

questions.q: What is the work function phi of a metal surface?
a: The total kinetic energy of emitted photoelectrons
The energy required to melt the metal
The maximum energy of a photon in a beam
The minimum energy required to liberate an electron from the surface of the metal

questions.q: What is Einstein's photoelectric equation relating maximum kinetic energy KE_max of emitted photoelectrons, photon energy hf, and work function phi?
What is stopping potential V_s in a photoelectric experiment defined as?
a: The voltage required to start photoemission
The minimum negative potential applied to the anode that stops even the most energetic photoelectrons from reaching it, such that e * V_s = KE_max
The potential difference across the metal plate
The ionization potential of gas atoms

questions.q: What does de Broglie's wavelength hypothesis state for a particle of momentum p (mass m, velocity v)?
Which phenomenon provides direct experimental evidence for the wave nature of electrons?
a: Electron diffraction (e.g., passing electrons through a thin graphite crystal)

questions.q: What happens to the maximum kinetic energy of emitted photoelectrons if the intensity of incident monochromatic light above threshold frequency is doubled?
a: Maximum kinetic energy remains unchanged (though number of emitted photoelectrons per second doubles)

questions.q: Why does wave theory fail to explain the photoelectric effect?
a: Wave theory predicts that light energy is localized in photons
Wave theory predicts that any frequency of light should cause emission given enough time for energy accumulation, which contradicts the existence of a threshold frequency
Wave theory predicts zero energy transfer
Wave theory accounts only for transverse waves

questions.q: What is the momentum p of a photon of frequency f and wavelength lambda?
a: p = h / lambda = h f / c

questions.q: What does a line emission spectrum from a low-pressure atomic gas indicate about electron energy levels in atoms?
a: Energy levels are continuous and unbounded
Electrons spiral freely into the nucleus
Energy levels can take any arbitrary value
Energy levels in atoms are discrete (quantized), and photons are emitted when electrons transition between higher and lower energy levels

What happens to line absorption spectra when white light passes through a cool, low-pressure gas?
a: Dark lines appear across the continuous spectrum corresponding exactly to photon frequencies absorbed by electrons jumping to higher energy levels
Bright colored lines appear on a black background

questions.q: What is the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons emitted from a metal of work function 2.0 eV when illuminated by ultraviolet light of photon energy 4.5 eV?
What is the energy change delta E when an electron transitions between two energy levels in an atom emitting a photon of frequency f?
a: delta E = h f = E_2 - E_1

questions.q: What is the stopping potential when photoelectrons with a maximum kinetic energy of 1.60 x 10⁻¹⁹ J are stopped by an opposing electric field? (e = 1.60 x 10⁻¹⁹ C)
Why do electrons exhibit diffraction effects similar to X-rays when passed through thin crystalline materials?
a: Because electrons have mass and charge
Because the de Broglie wavelength of accelerated electrons is comparable to the atomic spacing in crystals
Because electrons break down into smaller wave packets

questions.q: What is the momentum of a photon with a wavelength of 400 nm?
Which property of light is best explained by the wave model rather than the photon model?
a: Interference and diffraction of light waves

questions.q: What is the frequency of a photon whose energy is equal to 3.30 x 10⁻¹⁹ J? (h = 6.63 x 10⁻³⁴ J s)
What energy is required to accelerate an electron from rest through a potential difference of 100 V?
What is the de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 100 V?
a: 1.23 x 10⁻¹⁰ m (Wait: lambda = h / square root of (2 m e V) = 6.63e-34 / square root of (2 * 9.11e-31 * 1.60e-19 * 100) = 1.23e-10 m)

questions.q: What does wave-particle duality state in modern quantum mechanics?
a: All particles travel strictly at the speed of light
Light and matter exhibit both wave-like and particle-like properties depending on the experimental context
Waves and particles are completely independent physical phenomena
Mass can be converted into electrical charge

questions.q: What is the work function of a metal in electron-volts if its threshold frequency is 5.5 x 10¹⁴ Hz? (h = 6.63 x 10⁻³⁴ J s, 1 eV = 1.60 x 10⁻¹⁹ J)
What happens to the rate of emission of photoelectrons (photocurrent) when the intensity of incident ultraviolet light above threshold frequency is increased?
a: Current increases because more photons strike the metal surface per unit time, ejecting more photoelectrons

questions.q: What is the maximum speed of photoelectrons emitted when light of frequency 1.0 x 10¹⁵ Hz shines on a metal with a work function of 2.0 eV? (h = 6.63 x 10⁻³⁴ J s, m_e = 9.11 x 10⁻³¹ kg)
Why can optical microscopes not resolve objects smaller than approximately 200 nm, whereas electron microscopes can achieve atomic resolution?
a: Because visible light photons carry negative charge
Because optical lenses absorb ultraviolet rays
Because the de Broglie wavelength of accelerated electrons is much smaller than the wavelength of visible light, diffraction limits resolution

Interference fringes in Young's double-slit experiment
